newsitem.title: UK: Dollar backs off in Europe after setting new high.
newsitem.headline: Dollar backs off in Europe after setting new high.

text.p: The dollar took a breather in European trading Tuesday after charging to a 40-month high against the German mark in early trading as traders eyed the outcome of the Federal Reserve's latest policy-making meeting.

Although analysts polled by Reuters expect no rate change from the Fed's Open Market Committee on Tuesday or Wednesday, the dollar is supported by expectations of more U.S. interest rate rises further out.
Uncertainty about the size and make-up of European monetary union is keeping the German unit depressed, meantime, while the strength of sterling and the Italian lira also hit the mark.

"The dollar has been grinding out new highs but it has yet to make a decisive push to the upside and is prone to pullbacks like this," said Joe Prendergast, head of global foreign exchange research and strategy at CSFB in London.
Prendergast said he expects no near-term change in U.S. interest rates and sees much of the dollar/mark's day-to-day moves dicated by "cross currents."

Sterling's retreat from a five-year high at 2.9100 marks earlier ahead of Wednesday's UK budget and mark/lira's approach to levels likely to encounter official support were both factors behind the dollar stopping short of 1.75 marks, said dealers.

At 1516 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7410/15 marks compared with 1.7432/39 late Monday and a new high in the Far East at 1.7488. Against the yen, it was at 114.71/81 compared with 114.49/54 late yesterday.

Dealers said summer-holiday trading was beginning to crimp activity, even on the first day of the third quarter, and this left the day's moves subject to chart and option-related plays as much as any fundamental reasoning.
Dollar/yen ran into offers above stiff technical resistance about 115.10, while traders said talk of a large knock-out option expiry in dollar/mark was seeing spot attracted to 1.75.

Hong Kong markets are closed today and Wednesday for a public holiday period marking the former British colony's handover to China, while U.S. markets will be closed Friday for the Fourth of July celebrations.
The U.S. market closure Friday means the release of the key June employment report will be a day early on Thursday.

Signs of robust activity in the Chicago Purchasing Managers index and May new home sales report on Monday were offset today as the National Association of Purchasing Management showed a bigger-than-expected decline in its main activity index. The index fell to 55.7 from 57.1 in May and a forecast for 56.4.
"All currencies are suffering from being in the FOMC shadow, with markets waiting until they get the confirmation on rates," said Stewart Newnham, economist at First Chicago.
The FOMC's decision is expected shortly after European markets close on Wednesday.
Even though few expect rates to rise, the still brisk pace of the U.S. expansion will keep rate speculation ahead of the August FOMC meeting alive and keep the dollar buoyed.
Sterling too continues to feed off the prospect of higher UK interest rates on the horizon although it recoiled today as traders awaited the outcome of tomorrow's UK budget.

"Nothing but a sizeable fiscal tightening of around seven to eight billion pounds could make a meaningful dent to rate hike expectations and take the wind out of sterling's sails," said Don Smith, economist at HSBC Midland.
The market is currently expecting a total fiscal tightening in the region of four billion pounds.
News of a drop in the UK's June Purchasing Managers' index to 53.4 from 54.4 in May helped keep a lid on the pound today.
Mark/lira hovered close to new five-month lows about 972.20 but is shy of its notional 2.25 percent ERM limit near 968.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
